headline: Not yet. But the market just flinched.
summary: Record highs last Tuesday, a 3–8% rout in AI names on Thursday over a roughly $20 billion revenue shortfall at OpenAI, then a full rebound by Friday. Spending and valuations keep climbing while rates rise. Stretched, not broken. [2]

analysis: The S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time on Tuesday 6 October. Two days later the Financial Times reported that OpenAI's annualized revenue was about $50 billion at the end of September, not the $68 billion signalled a month earlier, and Nvidia fell 3%, Oracle nearly 6% and CoreWeave nearly 8% in one session. By Friday a Bloomberg report that OpenAI expects at least $70 billion by year-end had brought the buyers back. [1][2]

The spending has not blinked. The four largest hyperscalers guide to more than $700 billion of capital expenditure this year, Goldman Sachs puts global AI investment above $1 trillion for 2026, and Alphabet posted its first negative free cash flow since its 2004 IPO to fund its share. [4][7] OpenAI, meanwhile, is sounding out investors for at least $30 billion at roughly $1.4 trillion, 64% above the $852 billion it closed in March. [5][6]

The classic trigger is dearer money, and it has arrived: on 16 September the Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75–4%, its first hike in over three years, and 56% of CEOs tell PwC that AI has delivered neither revenue nor savings. Joachim Klement of Panmure Liberum told Bloomberg TV last week the bubble "will either burst in 2027 or in 2028". [8][4][3] Why 72 and not 90: Nvidia's revenue still more than doubled year over year, indices sit at records, and Thursday's dip was bought within a day. [2][4]
